You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Fed June Meeting Minutes Breakdown: Hawkish Dissent + AI Inflation Double Hit — How Smart Money Is Positioning

TEXT:
The Federal Reserve released the minutes from its June 16-17 FOMC meeting in the early hours of July 9 Beijing time . Overall, the tone was hawkish, but with notable internal divisions. The federal funds rate stayed unchanged at 3.50%-3.75%. Most participants viewed current policy as “somewhat restrictive,” while inflation remains significantly above the 2% target.
Pressures include energy supply shocks, Middle East geopolitical tensions, and AI-driven demand surges (chips, memory, power, and data centers). A few officials explicitly supported rate hikes this year, stressing that if inflation pressures persist, further tightening may be needed.
At the same time, the minutes acknowledged AI’s potential for long-term productivity gains, though short-term effects are limited. The Fed continued to emphasize its “data-dependent” approach, keeping flexibility open for future hikes or ad just ments. This “hawkish but leaves the door open” document immediately tightened nerves in the already high-level oscillating U.S. stock market.
I. Current Market Theme: AI Bull Market vs. Inflation Ghost
The U.S. stock market is still dominated by the AI supercycle. The S&P 500 is oscillating at high levels, supported by strong corporate earnings growth (2026 full-year expectations exceeding 25%). However, high valuations and sector concentration risks stand out.
After the minutes release, market focus quickly shifted to AI-related inflation transmission, geopolitical energy uncertainty, and Fed policy signals. Capital showed clear defensive rotation: some tech growth stocks faced short-term pressure, while financials, energy, and traditional value sectors displayed relative resilience.
Leveraged traders (especially Bitget UEX users) should pay special attention to potential upside in U.S. Treasury yields pressuring high-valuation assets, as well as amplified volatility in the night session. Overall, the minutes reinforced the possibility of “higher for longer,” but the internal divisions also leave room for imagination if data improves and policy pivots.
II. Recommended Watchlist (Directly Actionable, Based on Minutes Impact)
Based on the minutes, here’s a practical Watchlist (adjust dynamically with real-time data):
AI/Tech Growth (Neutral to Cautious — Buy on Dips Preferred) : NVDA (AI leader), AMD (chips), PLTR (data intelligence), TSLA (robotics + energy), AMZN / META (cloud + advertising)
Financials (Hawkish Tailwind) : JPM , BAC , GS — net interest margins expand in a high-rate environment, delivering steady returns
Energy/Inflation Hedges (Solid Defense) : XOM , CVX , OXY — supply shocks + surging data center power demand, dual drivers
Defensive/Value Stocks (Volatility Resistant) : PG , JNJ , LMT , RTX — downside protection + dividends
Small-Cap/Cyclical Reference : IWM (small-cap ETF)
Suggested Position Allocation : AI 40%, Financials & Energy 35%, Defensive 25%. This list covers the minutes’ two core themes (AI pressures + inflation hedging) and works well for a mix of spot and leveraged positions.
III. Detailed Investment Logic
The minutes highlight the Fed’s deep understanding of AI’s “double-edged sword” effect: in the short term, AI infrastructure expansion drives up power and hardware demand, intensifying inflation pressure. Over the long term, it is expected to ease supply-demand imbalances through productivity gains.
Short-term Strategy : Play both offense and defense. Prioritize adding to financials (widening NIMs) and energy (inflation hedge), while holding core AI positions and waiting for better entry points on pullbacks. Medium-term Opportunity : Once inflation cools and employment data stabilizes, AI growth stocks should regain valuation expansion momentum.
Risk management is critical: strictly control leverage (recommend no more than 30% of total capital), set dynamic stop-losses at 5-8%, and closely monitor U.S. stock night-session moves (Beijing time) along with upcoming July macro data (e.g., jobs report, CPI).
The overall logic centers on “quality first”: in a macro-uncertain environment, prioritize companies with strong cash flows, deep moats, and pricing power. Avoid blindly chasing highs.
IV. AI Data Centers: The Hidden “Power-Hungry Tiger” Opportunity
The minutes unusually highlighted the massive electricity consumption of AI data centers. This isn’t sci-fi — it’s a supply-chain revolution happening right now.
The sharp rise in data center power usage not only directly affects energy prices but can also ripple through broader supply chains. Smart investors are already positioning in upstream energy infrastructure and AI hardware suppliers, while watching for potential policy responses. Short term: inflation pressure. Medium to long term: productivity explosion once AI scales.
This is the golden window to build the energy + AI dual-mainline theme. Don’t just watch stock prices — look at the real world where data center lights stay on 24/7.
V. Summary & Outlook
The June FOMC minutes further confirm the Fed’s firm stance on inflation control in the Warsh era, while preserving data-driven flexibility. In an environment where AI-driven earnings growth and inflation pressures coexist, the foundation of the U.S. stock bull market remains intact, but sector rotation will accelerate.
Bitget UEX users can use leverage to capture short-term opportunities while building a balanced long-term portfolio: AI tech as the core, financials & energy as defense, and value stocks as the base. Keep tracking follow-up data and official comments, and maintain disciplined position management.
In the coming months, the interplay between the AI productivity narrative and the Fed’s policy path will continue to dominate market moves. Grasping high-conviction themes will be the key to winning.
